difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — needs precise vocabulary from two fields (literary structure and music) and a correct reading of the direction of the relation (closing : opening), with a near-synonym distractor (Cadence); about 1.5 minutes.
concept: Analogy: the relation (closing section : opening section of the same kind of work) carried over from literature to music.
stem:
Select the option that best completes the analogy.

*Epilogue* : *Prologue* :: *Coda* : ________

solution.quick: An epilogue closes a literary work and a prologue opens it, so the given pair is (closing section : opening section). A coda is the closing passage of a piece of music, so the blank must be the musical term for the opening section, which is an overture.

steps.title: Fix the relation in the given pair
steps.body: *Epilogue* is the concluding section added at the end of a play, novel or poem; *Prologue* is the introductory section placed before it. Both are structural parts of the same kind of work, and the first term is the closing part while the second term is the opening part. The relation is therefore (closing section : opening section of a work), in that order.

steps.title: Carry the relation over to the music pair
steps.body: *Coda* (Italian for 'tail') is the closing passage that rounds off a piece of music. It occupies the position of the first term, so the blank has to name the opening section of a musical work.

steps.title: Test each option against the required role
steps.body: An *overture* is the instrumental introduction that opens an opera, ballet or oratorio: an opening. A *cadence* is a closing chord formula at the end of a phrase or section: another ending. An *interlude* lies between two sections. A *refrain* is a line or passage that recurs. Only the overture is an opening.

steps.title: Check that the direction is preserved
steps.body: Epilogue : Prologue :: Coda : Overture reads closing : opening on both sides, so the analogy holds with the order of the terms unchanged.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: A cadence is a closing progression of chords at the end of a phrase or section. It is another kind of ending, like the coda itself, and not the opening that pairs with it.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: An interlude is a passage placed between two main sections. It is neither the closing nor the opening of the work.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: A refrain is a line or passage that recurs at intervals, such as the chorus of a song. It has no fixed place at the start of a work.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: An overture is the orchestral introduction that opens an opera or ballet. It is the opening counterpart of the coda, as the prologue is of the epilogue.

solution.commonTrap: Choosing *Cadence* because it is the music word most strongly tied to endings. That matches the role of *Coda* (an ending) instead of supplying the opposite end of the work, which is what *Prologue* does for *Epilogue*.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (undoing two successive folds by reflecting the punched point in each fold line) with 2–3 routine steps and a coordinate-geometry area calculation; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Paper folding: a hole through a folded stack unfolds into the images of the point under the reflections in the fold lines.
stem:
A square sheet of paper has corners $O(0,0)$, $P(8,0)$, $Q(8,8)$ and $R(0,8)$, with all lengths in cm. The sheet is folded twice. Coordinates always refer to the fixed plane in which the sheet lies.

1. **First fold:** along the diagonal $OQ$, so that corner $R$ lands on corner $P$. The part of the sheet containing $P$ stays in place, and the folded sheet is the right-angled triangle $OPQ$ (two layers).
2. **Second fold:** along the line through $P$ and the midpoint $M(4,4)$ of $OQ$, so that corner $O$ lands on corner $Q$. The part containing $Q$ stays in place, and the folded sheet is the triangle $PMQ$ (four layers).

A single hole is punched through all four layers at the point $(7,3)$ of the folded triangle $PMQ$, and the sheet is then completely unfolded. The four holes in the unfolded sheet are the vertices of a quadrilateral.

The area of this quadrilateral, in cm$^2$, is

solution.quick: Undo the folds in reverse order. Mirroring $(7,3)$ in the line $x+y=8$ gives $(5,1)$; mirroring both points in the line $y=x$ gives $(3,7)$ and $(1,5)$. The holes $(5,1),(7,3),(3,7),(1,5)$ form a rectangle with sides $2\sqrt2$ and $4\sqrt2$, so its area is $16$ cm$^2$.

steps.title: Undo the second fold
steps.body: The second fold mirrored triangle $OPM$ onto triangle $QPM$ in the line $PM$, which is $x+y=8$. Mirroring in this line sends $(x,y)$ to $(8-y,\,8-x)$. The hole at $(7,3)$ therefore also appears at $(8-3,\,8-7)=(5,1)$ in triangle $OPQ$. After this step the sheet is the two-layer triangle $OPQ$ with holes at $(7,3)$ and $(5,1)$.

steps.title: Undo the first fold
steps.body: The first fold mirrored triangle $ORQ$ onto triangle $OPQ$ in the line $OQ$, which is $y=x$. Mirroring in this line sends $(x,y)$ to $(y,x)$. The holes $(7,3)$ and $(5,1)$ therefore also appear at $(3,7)$ and $(1,5)$. The unfolded sheet has the four holes $(7,3),\ (5,1),\ (1,5),\ (3,7)$.

steps.title: Identify the quadrilateral
steps.body: Going around the holes in the order $(5,1)\to(7,3)\to(3,7)\to(1,5)$, the side vectors are $(2,2)$, $(-4,4)$, $(-2,-2)$ and $(4,-4)$. Opposite sides are equal and parallel, and $(2,2)\cdot(-4,4)=0$, so adjacent sides are perpendicular: the quadrilateral is a rectangle.

steps.title: Compute the area
steps.body: The side lengths are $\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{4^2+4^2}=4\sqrt2$. The area is $2\sqrt2\times4\sqrt2=16$ cm$^2$. The shoelace formula on the four vertices gives the same value.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: This takes the side lengths as the coordinate steps $2$ and $4$ instead of the Euclidean lengths $2\sqrt2$ and $4\sqrt2$, giving $2\times4=8$. The sides lie along diagonals, so their lengths are not the coordinate steps.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: The rectangle has sides $2\sqrt2$ and $4\sqrt2$, so the area is $16$ cm$^2$, confirmed by the shoelace formula.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: This applies the formula $\tfrac12 d_1 d_2$, which holds only when the diagonals are perpendicular. Here both diagonals have length $\sqrt{40}$ but they are not perpendicular (the dot product of $(-6,2)$ and $(-2,6)$ is $24\ne0$), so $\tfrac12\cdot40=20$ is wrong.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: This is the area $6\times6$ of the bounding square of the holes ($1\le x\le7$, $1\le y\le7$), not of the quadrilateral that they span.

solution.shortcut: A mirrored pair of holes lies at twice the distance of the point from the fold line. The distance from $(7,3)$ to $x+y=8$ is $\tfrac{2}{\sqrt2}$, giving a side of $2\sqrt2$, and to $y=x$ it is $\tfrac{4}{\sqrt2}$, giving a side of $4\sqrt2$. These two sides are perpendicular, so the area is $2\sqrt2\cdot4\sqrt2=16$.
solution.commonTrap: Using the point reflection $(x,y)\to(8-x,\,8-y)$ for the second fold instead of the reflection in the line $x+y=8$, or taking coordinate steps as side lengths (area $8$). Always reflect in the actual fold line, and use the Euclidean distance.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — a 2-mark inference question whose correct statement rests on a concession in the passage's last sentence, with distractors that reverse a stated fact, overstate the sceptics' position or add a comparison the passage never makes; about 3 minutes.
concept: Reading comprehension: inferring an author's reported position from a qualifying conclusion, and rejecting overstated or unsupported claims.
stem:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows.

> Ecologists use the phrase *shifting baseline* for a quiet distortion in how successive generations judge environmental loss. A fisheries biologist who begins work after cod stocks have already thinned treats the modest catches of her first seasons as normal; her successor, trained on her records, begins from a lower reference point still. No individual misreports anything, yet the yardstick against which decline is measured keeps sliding downward, so that a collapse spread over a century is never perceived as a single event. The usual remedy is to consult sources that predate living memory, such as ships' logs, old menus and museum specimens. Sceptics reply that such sources carry biases of their own: the logs were kept mostly where fishing was good, and museums collected mainly the large and the striking. The remedy, they conclude, narrows the distortion but cannot be assumed to remove it.

Which one of the following statements is best supported by the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Even the sceptics accept that consulting sources that predate living memory reduces the distortion, although they doubt that it removes it.

options.label: B
options.text: A shifting baseline develops because biologists misreport the catches that they observe in their own seasons.

options.label: C
options.text: According to the sceptics, sources that predate living memory are no more trustworthy than the observations of living biologists.

options.label: D
options.text: Museum specimens are a more dependable remedy than ships' logs because museums did not collect only where fishing was good.

solution.quick: The sceptics' conclusion is that the remedy 'narrows the distortion but cannot be assumed to remove it'. That concedes a partial benefit while doubting a complete cure, which is exactly statement A. B contradicts 'No individual misreports anything', C contradicts the narrowing, and D makes a comparison between specimens and logs that the passage never makes.

steps.title: Map the structure of the passage
steps.body: Sentences 1 to 3 define the shifting baseline: accurate observers, yet a reference point that slides lower with each generation. Sentence 4 gives the usual remedy (older sources). Sentences 5 and 6 report the sceptics' objection (older sources are biased too) and their conclusion.

steps.title: Read the sceptics' conclusion exactly
steps.body: The sceptics conclude that the remedy 'narrows the distortion but cannot be assumed to remove it'. The verb 'narrows' grants that the older sources do improve matters. The qualifier 'cannot be assumed to remove it' is their doubt about a complete cure. They therefore qualify the remedy and do not reject it.

steps.title: Test each statement against the text
steps.body: A restates the conclusion: a reduction is accepted, a full removal is doubted. B is contradicted by 'No individual misreports anything'. C is contradicted by the concession that the sources narrow the distortion. D compares museum specimens with ships' logs for dependability, but the passage only lists one bias for each and never ranks them.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Only statement A is supported by the text without adding or reversing anything.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Supported. The sceptics say the remedy 'narrows the distortion', which concedes a reduction, and that it 'cannot be assumed to remove it', which is the doubt about full removal.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Contradicted. The passage says 'No individual misreports anything'; the distortion arises from the sliding reference point, not from inaccurate reporting.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Contradicted. If the older sources were no more trustworthy than current observations, they could not 'narrow the distortion', yet the sceptics grant that they do.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Not supported. The passage names one bias for the logs and a different one for the museum specimens but never says that either source is more dependable than the other.

solution.commonTrap: Treating the sceptics as rejecting the remedy altogether because their part of the passage lists only objections. Their conclusion uses 'narrows', which concedes a benefit, so the question rewards reading the conclusion and not the tone of the objections.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (a clustering index on a non-key ordered field) needing the index size, a binary search over index blocks and the number of data blocks for one value, in 3–4 routine steps; about 2 minutes.
concept: Clustering index: sizing the index file and counting block accesses as a binary search over index blocks plus the contiguous data blocks of one value.
stem:
A university stores its `ENROLMENT` relation as a file of $72{,}000$ fixed-length records of $100$ bytes each. The disk block size is $1000$ bytes and records are **unspanned**. The file is physically ordered on the non-key attribute `dept_code`, which has $600$ distinct values, each occurring in exactly $120$ records.

A **clustering index** is built on `dept_code`. It has one entry for each distinct value of `dept_code`, consisting of a $6$-byte key and a $4$-byte block pointer to the first data block that contains that value. The index file is stored in blocks of $1000$ bytes (entries are unspanned) and is ordered on `dept_code`.

To retrieve all records with one given `dept_code`, the index file is searched by binary search over its blocks (this costs $\lceil \log_2 b \rceil$ block accesses for an index of $b$ blocks), and then the data blocks that hold those records are read.

The total number of block accesses needed is

solution.quick: An index entry takes $6+4=10$ bytes, so a block holds $100$ entries and the $600$ entries fill $6$ index blocks; binary search costs $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil=3$ accesses. A data block holds $10$ records, so the $120$ records of one value fill exactly $12$ consecutive blocks. Total $3+12=15$.

steps.title: Size the data file
steps.body: Records per data block $=\lfloor 1000/100\rfloor=10$. One `dept_code` value has $120$ records, which need $120/10=12$ blocks. The file is ordered on `dept_code`, starts at a block boundary and every value has exactly $120$ records, a multiple of $10$, so the records of each value occupy $12$ whole consecutive blocks.

steps.title: Size the index file
steps.body: An index entry is $6+4=10$ bytes, so a block holds $\lfloor 1000/10\rfloor=100$ entries. A clustering index has one entry per distinct value, i.e. $600$ entries, which need $600/100=6$ index blocks.

steps.title: Cost of finding the index entry
steps.body: Binary search over $b=6$ index blocks costs $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil=\lceil 2.585\rceil=3$ block accesses.

steps.title: Add the data-block reads
steps.body: The entry points to the first data block of the value. The records are contiguous, so reading all of them takes $12$ block accesses. The total is $3+12=15$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: This counts only the $12$ data blocks and ignores the cost of locating the index entry. The index file must be searched first.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: This charges a single access for the index. The index has $6$ blocks, and binary search over them needs $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil=3$ accesses, not $1$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Binary search over the $6$ index blocks costs $3$ accesses and the $12$ data blocks cost $12$, giving $3+12=15$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: This scans the $6$ index blocks one after another ($6+12=18$). The question states that the index is searched by binary search.

solution.commonTrap: Charging $1$ access (or none) for the index search, or reading the index blocks one after another instead of using binary search. Also remember that a clustering-index entry points only to the first block of a value, so all $12$ data blocks of that value must still be read.

answerVerification.independentAnswer: 15 (6 index blocks, 3 binary-search accesses + 12 data blocks)
answerVerification.checkCode:
import math
rec, rs, B, ent, nvals, per = 72000, 100, 1000, 6 + 4, 600, 120
bfr = B // rs
data_blocks = math.ceil(per / bfr)
assert all(len({i // bfr for i in range(d * per, (d + 1) * per)}) == data_blocks for d in range(nvals))
idx_blocks = math.ceil(nvals / (B // ent))
print(idx_blocks, data_blocks, math.ceil(math.log2(idx_blocks)) + data_blocks)
# prints: 6 12 15

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (extreme values of a differentiable function on a closed interval) in 3–4 routine steps: derivative, critical points, comparison of interior and endpoint values with exponentials; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Global maximum and minimum on a closed interval: compare the critical-point values with the endpoint values.
stem:
Let $f(x) = (x^2 - 3)\,e^{x}$ for $x \in [-4,\,2]$. Let $M$ and $m$ denote the maximum value and the minimum value of $f$ on this closed interval.

The value of $M - m$, rounded off to two decimal places, is ________.

solution.quick: $f'(x)=(x+3)(x-1)e^x$, so the critical points are $x=-3$ and $x=1$. Comparing $f(-4)\approx0.238$, $f(-3)\approx0.299$, $f(1)=-2e\approx-5.437$ and $f(2)=e^2\approx7.389$ gives $M=e^2$ (at the endpoint) and $m=-2e$. Hence $M-m=e^2+2e\approx12.83$.

steps.title: Find the critical points
steps.body: By the product rule, $f'(x)=2x\,e^x+(x^2-3)e^x=(x^2+2x-3)e^x=(x+3)(x-1)e^x$. Since $e^x>0$, $f'(x)=0$ exactly at $x=-3$ and $x=1$, and both lie in $[-4,2]$.

steps.title: Sign of $f'$ on the interval
steps.body: $f'>0$ on $(-4,-3)$, $f'<0$ on $(-3,1)$ and $f'>0$ on $(1,2]$. So $f$ rises to a local maximum at $x=-3$, falls to a local minimum at $x=1$, then rises again up to the endpoint $x=2$.

steps.title: Evaluate at the critical points and the endpoints
Pick the extreme values
steps.body: The largest of the four values is $f(2)=e^2$, so $M=e^2\approx7.3891$. The smallest is $f(1)=-2e$, so $m\approx-5.4366$. The local maximum at $x=-3$ is not the global maximum, because $f$ keeps increasing after $x=1$ and ends higher at $x=2$.

solution.commonTrap: Taking $M$ to be the local maximum value $f(-3)\approx0.2987$ and forgetting to test the endpoint $x=2$. That gives $0.2987+5.4366\approx5.74$. On a closed interval the global extremes can occur at the endpoints, so they must always be compared.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
f = lambda x: (x**2 - 3) * np.exp(x)
x = np.linspace(-4, 2, 6_000_001)
y = f(x)
print(round(float(y.max() - y.min()), 2), np.e**2 + 2 * np.e)
# prints: 12.83 12.82561975584874

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (linear search with a move-to-front list update) needing a nine-query trace in which the list changes after every successful search and an unsuccessful search costs a full scan; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Linear search with the move-to-front heuristic: counting comparisons over a query sequence while the list order changes.
stem:
The following Python program searches a list by linear search. When the key is found, it is moved to the front of the list (the *move-to-front* heuristic).

```python
def lookup(a, key):
    count = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        count += 1
        if a[i] == key:
            a.insert(0, a.pop(i))
            return count
    return count

a = [14, 27, 8, 31, 5, 19]
total = 0
for k in [8, 19, 8, 5, 31, 40, 5, 27, 19]:
    total += lookup(a, k)
print(total)
```

The value printed by the program is ________.

solution.quick: `lookup` returns the number of elements compared, and a successful search moves the key to the front, so the list order changes for later queries. Tracing the nine queries gives $3,6,2,6,6,6,2,6,5$ comparisons, whose sum is $42$.

steps.title: Understand `lookup`
steps.body: `count` is incremented once per element examined. A successful search stops at the key's position $p$ (1-based), costs $p$ comparisons, and moves the key to the front. An unsuccessful search (key $40$) examines all $6$ elements, costs $6$, and leaves the list unchanged.

steps.title: Add the comparison counts
steps.body: $total=3+6+2+6+6+6+2+6+5=42$. Each search costs at most $n=6$ comparisons, so the worst case for nine queries would be $9\times6=54$; the total is lower because repeated keys are found near the front.

solution.commonTrap: Using the positions in the original list for every query (giving $3+6+3+5+4+6+5+2+6=40$) and so ignoring that the list is rearranged after each successful search, or forgetting that the absent key $40$ still costs a full scan of $6$ comparisons.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (the nature of the target variable decides regression versus classification) applied to four statements, two of which carry a numeric-coding or probability-output trap; about 1.5 minutes.
concept: Regression versus classification: the problem type is set by whether the target is a continuous quantity or a categorical label, not by whether numbers appear.
stem: A data-science team is framing four prediction tasks. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Replacing a real-valued target such as monthly rent by one of three labels (low, medium, high), obtained from fixed thresholds, and then predicting the label turns the task from a regression problem into a classification problem.

options.label: B
options.text: A parcel's delivery zone is coded $1, 2, \ldots, 9$, with no meaningful order or distance between zones. Because the codes are numbers, predicting the zone of a parcel from its address is a regression problem.

options.label: C
options.text: A model that outputs the expected waiting time of a patient, such as $17.4$ minutes, solves a regression problem even if the waiting times recorded in the training data are whole numbers of minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: A model is trained to predict whether a customer will churn (yes or no) and outputs a churn probability such as $0.83$. Because its output is a real number between $0$ and $1$, this is a regression problem.

solution.quick: The problem type is decided by the target: a continuous, ordered quantity gives regression, and a label from a finite set of categories gives classification. Discretising rent into bands (A) and predicting a real-valued waiting time (C) are as stated. Numeric zone codes (B) and a probability output for a yes/no target (D) are numbers, but the targets are categories, so those are classification.

steps.title: State the criterion
steps.body: In supervised learning, **regression** predicts a continuous quantity (the target has numeric meaning: order and distance matter), while **classification** predicts one of a finite set of categories (labels). What matters is the nature of the target variable, not whether it is written with digits and not what form the model's raw output takes.

steps.title: Statements A and B
steps.body: A: after thresholding, the target is one of three categories (low, medium, high), so predicting it is classification; the original rent target would have been regression. A is correct. B: the codes $1,\dots,9$ are labels for unordered categories, so arithmetic on them is meaningless (zone $6$ is not 'twice' zone $3$ in any useful way). Predicting a category is classification, and B is incorrect.

steps.title: Statements C and D
steps.body: C: waiting time is a continuous quantity and the model outputs the real number $17.4$ as an estimate of it; recording the training targets in whole minutes only coarsens the measurement, so this is regression and C is correct. D: the target is a yes/no label, so the task is classification. The probability $0.83$ is an intermediate output (a score for the class 'churn') that is thresholded or used to rank customers, and D is incorrect.

steps.title: Collect the correct statements
steps.body: A and C are correct; B and D are incorrect.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. Cutting a continuous target into labelled bands makes the target categorical, so the task becomes classification.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. The zone codes are unordered category labels written as numbers. Predicting a category is classification, whatever the digits look like.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The target is a continuous quantity (time) and the model returns a real-valued estimate such as $17.4$; whole-minute recording only coarsens the data.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. The target is a yes/no label, so this is binary classification. The probability is a real-valued score for the class, not a regression target (logistic regression is a classification method despite its name, for the same reason).

solution.commonTrap: Deciding by whether the target or the output 'looks numeric'. Zone codes $1$ to $9$ and a probability $0.83$ are numbers, but the first is a category label and the second is a score for a categorical target, so both belong to classification.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — three linked constraints (mean, median, unique mode) need case analysis on how often the mode occurs and a bounding argument under repetition limits, with a likely trap about ties for the mode; about 4 minutes.
concept: Mean, median and unique mode of a small integer data set: case analysis and bounding to find an extreme possible value.
stem:
A data set of seven positive integers (repetition allowed) has mean $10$ and median $9$. Its mode is $7$, and the mode is **unique**: the value $7$ occurs more often than any other value, so no other value occurs as many times as $7$ does.

Over all such data sets, the smallest possible value of the largest of the seven integers is ________.

solution.quick: Sort the data as $a_1\le\dots\le a_7$: the sum is $70$ and $a_4=9$. The $7$s must sit among $a_1,a_2,a_3$ and occur $2$ or $3$ times, and no other value may occur as often. Making $a_1+a_2+a_3$ as large as possible ($21$ or $22$) and spreading the rest of the sum over $a_5,a_6,a_7$ under the repetition limit forces $a_7\ge14$, and $14$ is attainable.

steps.title: Translate the conditions
steps.body: Sorted, $a_1\le\dots\le a_7$, the mean $10$ gives $\sum a_i=70$ and the median $9$ gives $a_4=9$. Since $7<9$, every $7$ lies among $a_1,a_2,a_3$, so $7$ occurs $k=2$ or $k=3$ times, and every other value occurs fewer than $k$ times.

steps.title: Case $k=3$
steps.body: Then $a_1=a_2=a_3=7$, so $a_5+a_6+a_7=70-21-9=40$. Other values may occur at most twice. If $a_7=t$, the largest possible sum is $t+t+(t-1)=3t-1$, which must be at least $40$, so $t\ge 14$ (for $t=13$ the maximum is only $38$). Check $t=14$: $(7,7,7,9,12,14,14)$ has sum $70$, median $9$, and $7$ occurs three times against at most two for any other value.

steps.title: Case $k=2$
steps.body: The third small entry $x$ is either below $7$ or equal to $8$; it cannot be $9$, because two $9$s would tie with two $7$s. So $a_1+a_2+a_3\le 7+7+8=22$ and $a_5+a_6+a_7\ge70-9-22=39$. Now every other value may occur only once, and $9$ is already used, so $a_5<a_6<a_7$. With $a_7=t$ the largest possible sum is $t+(t-1)+(t-2)=3t-3\ge39$, so $t\ge14$ again. Check $t=14$: $(7,7,8,9,12,13,14)$ has sum $70$ and a unique mode $7$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: In both cases $a_7\ge14$, and $14$ is attained, so the smallest possible largest value is $14$.

solution.commonTrap: Allowing repeats that tie with the mode. For example $(7,7,8,9,13,13,13)$ has sum $70$ and median $9$, which would suggest $13$, but $13$ occurs three times and $7$ only twice, so $7$ is not the unique mode. The uniqueness condition caps how often every other value may repeat.

answerVerification.notes: Exhaustive enumeration of all non-decreasing 7-tuples of positive integers with sum 70 (119 qualify) confirms the minimum largest value is 14.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — Huffman coding over eight weighted symbols (seven merges with a tie at weight 15) compared with a fixed-length baseline; error-prone bookkeeping of sorted weights; about 4 minutes.
concept: Data compression: total length of a Huffman-coded column versus a fixed-length encoding.
stem:
A log table has a categorical column `event_type` with eight distinct values. Over $180$ rows, the number of rows holding each value is:

| Value | E1 | E2 | E3 | E4 | E5 | E6 | E7 | E8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rows | 6 | 9 | 13 | 15 | 21 | 26 | 34 | 56 |

The column is compressed by replacing each value with its **Huffman code**, built from these row counts (ties may be broken arbitrarily; the code table is stored separately and is not counted). It is compared with a fixed-length binary code of the smallest possible length for eight values.

The number of bits by which the Huffman-coded column is shorter than the fixed-length-coded column is ________.

solution.quick: A fixed-length code for $8$ values needs $3$ bits per row, so $180\times3=540$ bits. The total Huffman length equals the sum of the weights of all internal nodes created by the seven merges, $15+28+36+54+70+110+180=493$ bits. The saving is $540-493=47$ bits.

steps.title: Fixed-length baseline
steps.body: Eight distinct values need $\lceil\log_2 8\rceil=3$ bits each, so the column takes $3\times180=540$ bits.

steps.title: Build the Huffman tree by repeated merging
steps.body:
Always merge the two smallest weights.

| Step | Merge | New weight | Weights now present |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $6+9$ | 15 | 13, 15, 15, 21, 26, 34, 56 |
| 2 | $13+15$ | 28 | 15, 21, 26, 28, 34, 56 |
| 3 | $15+21$ | 36 | 26, 28, 34, 36, 56 |
| 4 | $26+28$ | 54 | 34, 36, 54, 56 |
| 5 | $34+36$ | 70 | 54, 56, 70 |
| 6 | $54+56$ | 110 | 70, 110 |
| 7 | $70+110$ | 180 | 180 |

In step 2 there are two weights equal to $15$ (the leaf E4 and the merged node); either choice gives the same total length.

steps.title: Total length of the Huffman-coded column
steps.body: Each merge adds one bit to every row below the merged node, so the total number of bits is the sum of all merged weights: $15+28+36+54+70+110+180=493$ bits (average code length $493/180\approx2.74$ bits per row).

steps.title: Compare with the fixed-length code
steps.body: The saving is $540-493=47$ bits.

solution.commonTrap: Mishandling the sorted order after a merge (for example combining $6+9$ and then leaving the new weight $15$ out of the next comparison), or comparing against the wrong baseline such as $8$ bits per value. The baseline here is $\lceil\log_2 8\rceil=3$ bits per row, and a Huffman tree's length is a sum of internal-node weights, not of the leaf weights.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import heapq, math
rows = [6, 9, 13, 15, 21, 26, 34, 56]
h = rows[:]
heapq.heapify(h)
huff = 0
while len(h) > 1:
    a, b = heapq.heappop(h), heapq.heappop(h)
    huff += a + b
    heapq.heappush(h, a + b)
fixed = math.ceil(math.log2(len(rows))) * sum(rows)
print(sum(rows), huff, fixed, fixed - huff)
# prints: 180 493 540 47
